name: OpenIE Research & Unsiloeing AAC Concepts Anchor
description: Machine-readable W3C SKOS and Schema.org DefinedTermSet anchor for screen readers, switches, and Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) devices. Every concept carries a <=20-word zero-jargon plainDefinition, one-idea Easy-Read sentences, and AAC core-vocabulary symbol hints.

hasDefinedTerm.plainDefinition: A safety check that runs before any permanent computer action and records yes or no.
hasDefinedTerm.sourceDefinition: A check that runs before an irreversible action. A proposal may not authorize itself. The gate commits or refuses and writes a receipt.
easyReadSentences: Some computer actions cannot be undone.
A commit gate checks safety before the computer acts.
If the check fails, the gate says no and writes down why.

relatedStudies.label: Thermodynamic Bounds and an Optimal Tempo

hasDefinedTerm.plainDefinition: A saved record showing what a computer predicted, what happened, and how much energy it used.
hasDefinedTerm.sourceDefinition: A record written for every decision: the prediction and its timestamp before the act, the outcome, the match, the joules by label, and the refusal reason if any.
easyReadSentences: Every important computer choice leaves a written receipt.
The receipt shows what was expected and how much power was used.
Anyone can check the receipt later to verify honesty.

hasDefinedTerm.plainDefinition: A clear pass-or-fail test that checks whether a job is truly finished.
hasDefinedTerm.sourceDefinition: A written test that maps the state z of a task to 0 or 1, for example tests pass, a proof checks, or an output matches a reference. A task is complete when C(z) = 1.
easyReadSentences: A computer needs a clear rule to know when a job is done.
This test gives one for pass and zero for fail.
No system gets credit until it passes the test.

relatedStudies.label: Thermodynamic Bounds and an Optimal Tempo

hasDefinedTerm.plainDefinition: The smallest amount of electrical energy needed to finish a job right.
hasDefinedTerm.sourceDefinition: The least expected energy, in joules (J), that a system needs to reach C(z) = 1 with failure probability at most δ. Systems that pass are ordered by J*; ordering by a real number is a total preorder.
easyReadSentences: First, a computer must finish the job the right way.
Next, we count the electrical energy it spent in joules.
Spending less energy for the same right answer is smarter.

relatedStudies.label: Thermodynamic Bounds and an Optimal Tempo

hasDefinedTerm.plainDefinition: How much looking up a new clue improves your choice, minus the cost of looking.
hasDefinedTerm.sourceDefinition: The expected gain in a decision's payoff from observing a quantity before deciding, minus the cost of observing it (Howard, 1966).
easyReadSentences: Looking for extra clues takes time and power.
Sometimes a clue helps you make a much better choice.
If checking costs more than it helps, stop and decide now.

relatedStudies.label: Thermodynamic Bounds and an Optimal Tempo

hasDefinedTerm.plainDefinition: Extra computer work wasted when two machines swap text meant for human eyes.
hasDefinedTerm.sourceDefinition: The extra work a machine consumer does because information arrives in a format made for people to read: encode, parse, tokenize and, for a model, read the extra tokens. Defined with units in "AI" Reads Human; no joule value is claimed for it yet.
easyReadSentences: People like reading spaced words and punctuation.
Machines work much faster with compact numbers.
Forcing two machines to read human text wastes extra power.

hasDefinedTerm.plainDefinition: A small word piece that a language model reads one step at a time.
hasDefinedTerm.sourceDefinition: The unit a language model reads, a piece of text produced by a tokenizer. The same records give different token counts in different formats and under different tokenizers.
easyReadSentences: Language models chop sentences into small word pieces.
Each small piece is called a token.
More tokens mean the computer must do more work.

relatedStudies.label: The Promised Trillion Dollar AI-Coding Market

hasDefinedTerm.plainDefinition: The tiny physical floor of heat released whenever one bit of memory is erased.
hasDefinedTerm.sourceDefinition: The minimum heat dissipated by erasing one bit at temperature T: k_B T ln 2, about 2.87 × 10⁻²¹ J at 300 K (Landauer, 1961).
easyReadSentences: Wiping one bit of computer memory releases a tiny bit of heat.
Physics sets a floor that no machine can go below.
Real computers today still spend far more power than this floor.

relatedStudies.label: Thermodynamic Bounds and an Optimal Tempo

hasDefinedTerm.plainDefinition: Trying quick low-power tools first and waking giant models only when simple tools miss.
hasDefinedTerm.sourceDefinition: An order of mechanisms (gears) tried from lowest to highest expected energy, stopping at the first that passes the check. Expected energy is minimized by trying gears in decreasing order of p_i / c_i, with p_i the pass probability and c_i the expected energy (Simon and Kadane, 1975).
easyReadSentences: Start every job with the smallest, fastest tool.
If the small tool passes the check, stop right there.
Wake up a giant model only for brand-new hard problems.

hasDefinedTerm.plainDefinition: Using the lowest-energy tool that passes the test and stopping as soon as it works.
hasDefinedTerm.sourceDefinition: The rule of using the cheapest gear that passes the check and stopping when further spend cannot change C(z). The cheapest-first cascade is one instance.
easyReadSentences: Different tools use very different amounts of electricity.
Pick the cheapest tool that solves the task cleanly.
Stop spending power once the right answer is checked.

hasDefinedTerm.plainDefinition: A rule that picks the next step with the best chance per unit of energy.
hasDefinedTerm.sourceDefinition: A selector that picks the next act by the ratio of pass probability to energy cost and stops when the next act's expected gain is below its energy cost.
easyReadSentences: A computer may have several ways to try a task.
This rule compares chance of success against energy cost.
It stops when trying again is not worth the power.

relatedStudies.label: Thermodynamic Bounds and an Optimal Tempo

hasDefinedTerm.plainDefinition: The finish line where spending more power or words cannot improve the answer.
hasDefinedTerm.sourceDefinition: The least spend that closes a task. Past it, further tokens, parameters or joules cannot change C(z).
easyReadSentences: Once a job is solved right, extra work adds nothing.
That flat finish line is called the plateau.
Smart systems stop right at the finish line.

relatedStudies.label: Thermodynamic Bounds and an Optimal Tempo

hasDefinedTerm.plainDefinition: An honest label showing whether an answer came from an exact rule or a guessing model.
hasDefinedTerm.sourceDefinition: A label on an answer stating how it was produced. An answer labeled ModelGenerated cannot be relabeled Deterministic.
easyReadSentences: Some answers come from exact math rules.
Other answers are guesses from a language model.
This label keeps guesses from pretending to be exact rules.

hasDefinedTerm.plainDefinition: A working computer program used to test rules before attaching physical power sensors.
hasDefinedTerm.sourceDefinition: The software used to test a claim without board-level metering. Its energy figures are estimates.
easyReadSentences: Engineers write a clear test program first.
Everyone can run the program to check the rules.
Its power numbers are software estimates, not wire readings.

hasDefinedTerm.plainDefinition: A math estimate of energy found by multiplying step counts by known step costs.
hasDefinedTerm.sourceDefinition: An analytical energy estimate: operation counts times stated energy constants, in joules.
easyReadSentences: Sometimes we count how many small steps a chip takes.
We multiply those steps by a stated power formula.
This label marks the number as a math estimate.

hasDefinedTerm.plainDefinition: An energy reading reported by a computer chip's built-in power counter.
hasDefinedTerm.sourceDefinition: An energy figure read from an operating-system or on-chip counter, such as RAPL package energy minus a stated idle baseline.
easyReadSentences: Many modern computer chips have built-in energy counters.
Software can read those counters before and after a task.
This label marks chip-counter readings separately from wire sensors.

hasDefinedTerm.plainDefinition: A real electrical energy reading taken from a physical sensor on a power wire.
hasDefinedTerm.sourceDefinition: A joule reading from a wall or shunt meter on a named rail, with its calibration stated. Never summed with reported_j, est_j or trajectory_j. Metered Commit Gates also files its KV260 (AMD Kria) onboard INA260 (power monitor) differences under this label, and states that those readings are whole-module, not a core rail.
easyReadSentences: A physical power sensor sits right on the circuit board.
It measures real electrical current flowing into the hardware.
We never mix these wire readings with software guesses.

hasDefinedTerm.plainDefinition: Tiny physical work calculated from tracked motion paths at the scale of molecules.
hasDefinedTerm.sourceDefinition: Work computed from measured physical trajectories and a calibrated potential, for physical act cycles near the k_B T scale.
easyReadSentences: Tiny moving parts follow measurable paths through space.
Physics formulas turn those motion paths into work.
This label marks tiny motion energy near room heat.

relatedStudies.label: Thermodynamic Bounds and an Optimal Tempo

hasDefinedTerm.plainDefinition: Three honest labels showing whether a result came from math, simulation, or real hardware.
hasDefinedTerm.sourceDefinition: Modeled: a stated formula. Simulated: a program or hardware-description run. Measured: a named meter on a stated device and workload.
easyReadSentences: Modeled means calculated from a written formula.
Simulated means tested inside a computer program.
Measured means read from a real sensor on named hardware.

hasDefinedTerm.plainDefinition: A true-or-false badge that is true only when real circuit-board power sensors were used.
hasDefinedTerm.sourceDefinition: A page flag that is true only when a labeled meter returned a board energy reading for that paper.
easyReadSentences: Most software studies do not attach physical wire sensors.
Those studies set this badge to false for honesty.
It turns true only when real board sensors recorded power.

hasDefinedTerm.plainDefinition: Writing a program as clear states, allowed events, and a complete step-by-step log.
hasDefinedTerm.sourceDefinition: A program written as a state machine P = (S, E, δ, D, λ): states, events, a pure step function, an append-only log whose fold is the state, and outputs. The form is that shape (Gurevich's Abstract State Machine theorem); the fit is a program's vocabulary, rules and initial state.
easyReadSentences: Form is the clean shape of states and step rules.
Fit is the specific words and starting state for your job.
Together they leave nowhere for surprise bugs to hide.

hasDefinedTerm.plainDefinition: A system where you write one checked blueprint and get matching code in many languages.
hasDefinedTerm.sourceDefinition: A programming system, studied in its own paper, in which a program is written once as a Form and code in other languages is generated from it.
easyReadSentences: You write your program once as one clear blueprint.
A strict checker verifies every input has a safe outcome.
Then the engine builds matching code in several languages.

hasDefinedTerm.plainDefinition: A clear message naming the exact line and rule to fix before code can run.
hasDefinedTerm.sourceDefinition: The verdict of the RCE checker on code that is not in Form: the checker names the rule the code breaks, for example `requires change FILE: line 1: W-SYN-1 ...`, and nothing runs until the code is changed.
easyReadSentences: Broken blueprints are stopped before they can run.
The checker points to the exact rule that needs fixing.
Once you fix that rule, the blueprint can pass.

hasDefinedTerm.plainDefinition: When an invalid event arrives, the program keeps its old state safe and logs why.
hasDefinedTerm.sourceDefinition: A step whose event does not apply in the current state. The step keeps the state, unchanged (theorem T8, atomicity), and is recorded in the log with the error it names.
easyReadSentences: Sometimes an outside event does not fit the current state.
Instead of crashing, the program stays right where it was.
It writes down the skipped event in the log.

hasDefinedTerm.plainDefinition: Computer intelligence built to give the best checked answer inside a strict energy budget.
hasDefinedTerm.sourceDefinition: A class of computer intelligence designed to run inside a fixed energy budget B, studied in its own white paper.
easyReadSentences: Living things survive by respecting strict energy budgets.
Metabolic Intelligence gives computers a clear power limit up front.
In low battery, routine chatter pauses so urgent alerts survive.

hasDefinedTerm.plainDefinition: Open software in Rust that checks safety gates and writes receipts before actions run.
hasDefinedTerm.sourceDefinition: The Rust software implementation of the commit gate studied in Metered Commit Gates, Part I.
easyReadSentences: This open software guards actions before they happen.
It runs fast safety checks and logs energy receipts.
Anyone can inspect and run its code for free.

hasDefinedTerm.plainDefinition: A proposed definition of an agent that holds a goal, respects energy, and can refuse.
hasDefinedTerm.sourceDefinition: A proposed definition of an agent with an energy budget and a refusal rule, stated in the agency paper. It is a proposal.
easyReadSentences: An agent aims at a goal and acts on the world.
It must stay inside its available energy budget.
If an action breaks its budget, it can safely refuse.

relatedStudies.label: Thermodynamic Bounds and an Optimal Tempo

hasDefinedTerm.plainDefinition: Admitting code edits from many writers at once whenever a named checker approves them.
hasDefinedTerm.sourceDefinition: The statement quoted in the RCE-VC study: version control is admission of changes to one canonical, name-free repository state. A named checker accepts the post-state under a declared contract, or the change is refused with a recorded reason. Changes whose dependency closures do not meet are admitted without coordination. A stated cost ranks the admissible results. Every accepted result, including every resolved conflict, is reused. The study does not claim that existing version-control tools already work this way, and the reference is not the Reality Code Engine language.
easyReadSentences: Many people and computers can send code edits together.
A named checker tests whether the new state works.
Unrelated edits merge cleanly without fighting over line numbers.

hasDefinedTerm.plainDefinition: A frozen lookup table with zero models, used as a fair baseline test for AI.
hasDefinedTerm.sourceDefinition: A zero-model-call 64-bit integer case loop (OBSERVE, REDUCE, FUZZ, LOOKUP, ACT, VERIFY, MUTATE, WRITE) frozen before evaluation under SHA-256, OpenTimestamps, and drand randomness, used as the baseline control (strict N0 and dev-crystallized N1) against neural and agentic substrates.
easyReadSentences: Medicine tests new pills against a simple sugar pill.
This frozen lookup table is the fair baseline for AI.
It shows which tasks simple memory lookup already solves.

hasDefinedTerm.plainDefinition: Counting one-time requests to estimate how often the next request will be brand new.
hasDefinedTerm.sourceDefinition: The fraction of singleton keys observed along a task stream of length t (Good, 1953), estimating the probability that the next arriving task key has not yet been seen in the case store.
easyReadSentences: Some questions show up only once in a long stream.
Counting one-time questions tells us how much novelty remains.
When novelty drops, saved lookup answers handle most work.

hasDefinedTerm.plainDefinition: One verified master record from which papers, videos, audio, translations, and accessible formats grow.
hasDefinedTerm.sourceDefinition: One verified master record from which papers, videos, audio, translations, and accessible formats grow.
easyReadSentences: Previously, videos, papers, and datasets lived in separate boxes.
Now one verified master record connects every format together.
Screen readers, videos, and translations share the same truth.

hasDefinedTerm.plainDefinition: A signed digital wrapper that proves who made a file and that nothing was altered.
hasDefinedTerm.sourceDefinition: A signed digital wrapper that proves who made a file and that nothing was altered.
easyReadSentences: Files travel across websites, podcasts, and tools.
This wrapper locks the file with a digital fingerprint.
Any receiver can verify the file was never tampered with.

hasDefinedTerm.plainDefinition: A clear companion version using short one-idea sentences, everyday words, and helpful picture symbols.
hasDefinedTerm.sourceDefinition: A clear companion version using short one-idea sentences, everyday words, and helpful picture symbols.
easyReadSentences: Science belongs to everyone, not just specialists.
Easy Read uses short sentences with one idea each.
Picture symbols help readers and communication boards follow fast.

hasDefinedTerm.plainDefinition: A spoken voice track that describes on-screen shapes, colors, and motion for blind viewers.
hasDefinedTerm.sourceDefinition: A spoken voice track that describes on-screen shapes, colors, and motion for blind viewers.
easyReadSentences: Videos show moving charts and three-dimensional models.
Audio description speaks what appears on the screen.
Blind and low-vision listeners get the full visual story.

hasDefinedTerm.plainDefinition: A tiny sixteen-kilobyte lookup core sharing the sixty-four-state pattern of living genetic code.
hasDefinedTerm.sourceDefinition: A tiny sixteen-kilobyte lookup core sharing the sixty-four-state pattern of living genetic code.
easyReadSentences: Living cells use sixty-four triplets to store survival rules.
Digital six-input lookup tables also have sixty-four switches.
Grouping four neighbor switches together blocks small sensor noise.

hasDefinedTerm.plainDefinition: How living cells and computer teams scale up by sharing checked signals only when needed.
hasDefinedTerm.sourceDefinition: How living cells and computer teams scale up by sharing checked signals only when needed.
easyReadSentences: Constant noisy chatter wastes energy in cells and computers.
Smart groups speak only when a clear threshold is crossed.
Signed checks let ten specialist methods work as one team.
